title: The Impossible Task of Inclusion in Secondary Schools
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien questions whether current inclusion policy works in secondary schools, arguing that placing every student in the mainstream class regardless of attainment is promised as best for all but is stretching teachers beyond what they can deliver. He shows how a Victorian primary school with one main teacher differs structurally from a Year 10 student with six subject teachers, none of whom has been given time for the required documentation. He points to rising disability adjustment figures and to class attainment gaps that can span up to a decade, which make solid tier 1 instruction almost impossible. He adds that subject-expert secondary teachers rarely have the knowledge to teach decoding or number sense, and that modified curricula often become busywork while withdrawal for intervention costs students other learning. He concludes that the system may lower expectations for the very students it means to protect, while offering no neat solution.
points: Inclusion as practised in secondary schools places teachers in an impossible position when a single class spans up to ten years of attainment.
The Victorian documentation process is one-size-fits-all, loading secondary teachers with unpaid paperwork that primary teachers do not face in the same way.
Most secondary teachers are domain experts without training in literacy and numeracy foundations, so they cannot support students who cannot decode or lack number facts.
Modified curricula and withdrawal interventions tend to lower the bar or remove students from the learning everyone else receives.
The author fears mainstream inclusion with automatic promotion limits these students' future opportunities, and calls the problem structural.
quotes: Yet in the secondary school system we see year after year that the achievement gap in students continues to get wider. Despite teachers best efforts when the spread of attainment in their secondary class can cover upwards of 10 academic years with representation of each year in-between it creates a scenario where they cannot possible give any more without taking away from somewhere else. It’s stealing from Peter to pay Paul.

In comparison in Year 10 in the school I currently teach within a student will have 6 teachers for 6 different subjects who all have the student for an equal amount of time. This means that all teachers technically should have an equal say in the planning for and goal setting to promote the inclusive teaching of that particular student.

The large majority of secondary school teachers have elected to teach at a secondary level because they are relative experts in their domain. This may be Psychology, Business Studies or even English at a senior level. This means that when teachers are presented with a student who is unable to decode text that the teacher does not even know where to start in terms of the adjustments they implement in class.

Furthermore, in some cases schools will employ a literacy and numeracy specialist within the school to help with some of these tier 3 interventions to help develop and facilitate growth in those key areas. But when does this happen? Ironically it is often achieved by excluding them from their regular classes which then causes their knowledge and conceptual understanding of everything else to suffer.

I do know however that just giving funding to schools does not always equate to programs or tools which move the needle at all. This is a structural issue and one that does not look like it is going away any time soon.
